column2: For pregnant women and young children, the yolk must not stay runny.
You can make the sauce the day before and just cook the eggs in the morning.
Serve hot in the pan with fresh bread.
Wholemeal wrap with avocado and hummus
2 wholemeal lavash wraps
4 tablespoons hummus
Mash the avocado and mix with lemon juice and chilli flakes.
Slice the tomato thinly; wash and dry the rocket.
Spread hummus down the middle of each wrap.
Divide the avocado, tomato and rocket between them.
Fold up the bottom end, roll up tightly and cut in half.
Add a boiled egg or white cheese to boost the protein.
Wrap in foil for a school or work lunch box.
Eat within a few hours.
Red pepper and cheese breakfast muffins
Preheat the oven to 180°C; grease the muffin tin or use paper cases.
Dice the pepper small, chop the dill and crumble the cheese.
Whisk the eggs, yoghurt, milk and oil.
Add the flour and baking powder and stir a few times.
Add the pepper, cheese and dill; fill the tins two-thirds full.
Bake for 20–22 minutes, until golden on top and a toothpick comes out dry.
The cheese is salty, so no extra salt is needed.
Freeze them and reheat quickly in the morning.
Serve with tea and seasonal vegetables.
Keeps 3 days in a closed container in the fridge; 1 month in the freezer.
Avocado and banana purée
1–2 tablespoons breast milk or the baby’s usual formula
Wash your hands and the utensils you’ll use thoroughly.
Halve the avocado, remove the stone and scoop out the flesh of one half.
Peel the banana and mash it with the avocado using a fork until smooth.
Thin with breast milk or formula to a soft texture the baby can take from a spoon.
Serve immediately; avocado darkens as it stands.
Avocado contains healthy fats; it can be offered on its own at first.
Don’t add sugar, honey or salt.
Use straight away; don’t keep leftovers.
Pumpkin and lentil soup
1 slice of pumpkin (about 80 g)
Wash the lentils several times; peel the pumpkin and carrot and dice small.
Put all the ingredients in a pan with the water and bring to the boil; skim off the foam.
Cook over low heat for 20–25 minutes until the lentils break down and the vegetables are soft.
Blend and adjust to a consistency that runs off a spoon.
Stir in the olive oil and let it cool; check the temperature on the inside of your wrist.
Lentils are a source of iron and protein; a vitamin C-rich fruit alongside boosts absorption.
Apple oat porridge (baby)
3 tablespoons fine rolled oats
3–4 tablespoons breast milk or formula
Peel and core the apple and grate it finely.
Put the oats, apple and water in a small pan.
Cook over low heat, stirring constantly, for 5–6 minutes until the oats are soft.
Take off the heat and adjust the consistency with breast milk or formula.
In the first months blend it smooth; later, mashing with a fork is enough.
Oats may contain gluten; when introducing them, don’t add other new foods for 3 days.
Don’t add sugar; the apple sweetens it.
Serve fresh; keep leftovers in the fridge for 24 hours.
Broccoli and potato purée
4–5 broccoli florets
Peel and dice the potato; wash the broccoli and break into small florets.
Steam the potato for 10 minutes, then add the broccoli and steam for 5–6 minutes more.
When the vegetables mash easily with a fork, set aside the steaming water.
Mash with a blender or fork; add the cooking water a spoonful at a time to adjust the consistency.
Stir in the olive oil and serve lukewarm.
Steaming reduces vitamin loss.
As the baby grows, gradually leave the purée lumpier.
Pear quinoa porridge
Rinse the quinoa well under plenty of water in a fine sieve; this removes the bitter taste.
Bring the quinoa to the boil in the water and simmer for 15 minutes until soft.
Peel and chop the pear small and add it for the last 5 minutes.
Blend and adjust the consistency with boiled water.
Add a pinch of cinnamon if you like and serve lukewarm.
Quinoa is gluten-free and contains protein.
